conversation.content: Let's design a real-time chat system. Think about a messaging platform where users can send messages to each other. What questions do you have?

Exciting problem! So I'm thinking something like Slack or Discord. We'd want 1:1 messaging, group chats, channels, threads within channels, reactions, file sharing, and probably voice and video calling too. And screen sharing for the video calls. Oh, and we should think about bots and integrations — webhooks, slash commands. What's the scale we're targeting?

That's a lot of features. Let's start much simpler — I want you to focus on 1:1 text messaging only. Two users sending text messages to each other in real time. Let's nail that first. Scale: 50 million DAU, 500 million messages per day.

Got it, 1:1 text messaging. But I do think we should at least consider group messaging in our data model design so we don't paint ourselves into a corner. And message delivery guarantees — we need read receipts, delivered receipts, typing indicators. Also, we should think about end-to-end encryption from the start because retrofitting it later is a nightmare. And message search — users will want to search their chat history.

I appreciate the forward thinking, but you're expanding scope again. For this interview, I need you to focus on: sending a text message from User A to User B, and User B receiving it in real time. That's it. Can you start with the capacity estimation and high-level architecture for just that?

Right, sorry. Let me focus. 50M DAU, 500M messages per day. That's about 10 messages per active user per day, which seems reasonable. 500M messages per day is roughly 5,800 messages per second on average, probably 3x during peak so about 17,400 messages per second peak. Each message is maybe 200 bytes of text plus metadata — sender, receiver, timestamp, message ID — call it 500 bytes total. Storage: 500M * 500 bytes = 250 GB per day, about 91 TB per year. For connections: 50M users connected simultaneously via WebSocket.
Good numbers. Now the high-level architecture.

Okay. The key components are: a WebSocket gateway layer that maintains persistent connections with clients. Behind that, a message routing service that determines which gateway server the recipient is connected to. A message store for persistence. And a presence service to track who's online. Actually, for presence, we could also build a full social graph presence system where you see which of your contacts are online, their status (available, busy, do not disturb), custom status messages with emoji...
Focus. WebSocket gateway, message routing, message store. That's great. Tell me more about the WebSocket gateway layer.

Right. The WebSocket gateway is a fleet of servers that maintain long-lived connections. With 50M concurrent users, if each server handles 50K connections, we need about 1,000 gateway servers. When User A connects, they establish a WebSocket to one of these servers. The load balancer assigns them — could be based on a consistent hash of user ID or just round-robin with sticky sessions. Each gateway server registers which users it's handling in a distributed registry — Redis or a dedicated service discovery system.
Good. Now walk me through the message flow: User A sends 'Hello' to User B.

User A's client sends the message over their WebSocket to Gateway Server 3 (where A is connected). Gateway Server 3 passes it to the Message Service. The Message Service: 1) Assigns a unique message ID and timestamp. 2) Persists the message to the message store. 3) Looks up which gateway server User B is connected to — say Gateway Server 7, found via the Redis registry. 4) Routes the message to Gateway Server 7. 5) Gateway Server 7 pushes the message down User B's WebSocket. 6) User A gets an acknowledgment that the message was sent. This all should happen in under 100ms for the real-time feel.
What if User B is offline?

If User B isn't connected to any gateway, the message is still persisted in the message store. When User B comes back online and connects, they do a sync — pull all messages they haven't received since their last known message ID or timestamp. We could also add push notifications — when the routing step finds User B is offline, fire a push notification via APNs or FCM. Actually, for push notifications, we'd want a whole notification service with templates, batching, quiet hours, per-conversation mute settings, notification channels, snooze functionality...
You're creeping scope again. Message stored, User B syncs on reconnect, push notification fires. That's sufficient. Let's talk about the message store. What database?

Sorry about that. For the message store, the access pattern is: write a message, and read messages for a conversation in reverse chronological order. This is a time-series-like pattern. I'd use Cassandra. Partition key would be conversation_id (a deterministic hash of the two user IDs), clustering key would be message_timestamp DESC. This gives us efficient writes (append-only) and efficient reads (sequential scan within a partition). At 5,800 writes per second, Cassandra handles this easily. A 3-node cluster with RF=3 gives us durability and availability.
What happens if a conversation gets very long — millions of messages? Does the Cassandra partition get too large?

Yes, that's the unbounded partition problem. If two users chat for years, the partition could grow to hundreds of MB or even GB. Cassandra recommends keeping partitions under 100 MB. Solution: add a time bucket to the partition key. So the key becomes (conversation_id, month_year). Each month gets its own partition. When reading, we query the most recent bucket first, and paginate backwards across buckets as needed. This keeps partitions bounded while still allowing efficient reads of recent messages.
Good solution. How do you handle message ordering? What if two messages are sent at nearly the same time?

Timestamp alone isn't reliable for ordering because of clock skew across servers. I'd use a combination: each message gets a server-assigned timestamp AND a sequence number per conversation. The Message Service maintains a per-conversation sequence counter — could be in Redis with INCR. The sequence number provides a total order within a conversation. For display, sort by sequence number. If two messages arrive at the same instant, the one that got the lower sequence number appears first. It's a simple monotonically increasing counter.
Now, the routing layer — how does Gateway Server 3 send a message to Gateway Server 7 efficiently?

A few options. Option 1: Direct server-to-server communication. Gateway 3 looks up Gateway 7's address and sends an RPC directly. Simple but creates N^2 connections between gateway servers. Option 2: Message broker. Gateway 3 publishes to a Kafka topic or Redis pub/sub channel keyed by the target gateway server. Each gateway subscribes to its own channel. Option 3: Internal message bus. I'd go with Option 2 using Redis pub/sub for simplicity and low latency. Channel name is gateway:{server_id}. Gateway 7 subscribes to gateway:7 and receives messages for all its connected users.
What happens if a gateway server crashes? It has 50K connected users — what's the recovery path?

When a gateway crashes, all 50K WebSocket connections drop. The clients detect the disconnect and automatically reconnect — this is standard in any WebSocket client library, exponential backoff with jitter. They'll connect to a different gateway server. The new gateway updates the Redis registry with the new mapping. Any messages sent to the old gateway during the brief downtime would fail to deliver via pub/sub — but since messages are persisted first, the client picks them up during the reconnect sync. The user might see a brief 'reconnecting...' indicator but no messages are lost.
Good. Any final thoughts?

For production readiness: monitoring on message delivery latency (P50, P99), WebSocket connection counts per gateway, Cassandra write latency, and Redis pub/sub lag. Rate limiting on message sends to prevent spam. And I'd design the conversation_id and message schema to be extensible for group chat later — but I won't go into that now since we're focused on 1:1.

Good self-correction at the end. Honestly, you have strong technical depth, but you burned a lot of our time trying to expand scope. In a real interview, that pattern signals you might struggle with prioritization on the job. Thanks for the discussion.

strengths: Excellent Cassandra schema design with time bucketing for unbounded partitions
Strong message routing architecture with clear trade-off analysis
Good failure handling — gateway crash recovery is well thought out
weaknesses: Repeatedly expanded scope despite interviewer redirecting — happened four times
Poor prioritization signal — staff candidates should excel at scoping
Lost 8-10 minutes of interview time to scope discussions
Never got to discuss encryption, security, or multi-device sync due to time wasted
Pattern of feature-stuffing suggests difficulty shipping incrementally
